stops.narrative: Separate Sa‘di’s poem, copying likely in Herat and painting probably in Bukhara. Keep the catalogue’s uncertainty visible.
Inspect the birds on the Iznik dish, then choose the tughra. Compare material, use and specialized work rather than treating every object as a palace commission.
Read the carpet as costly craft within a wider silk economy. Bring New Julfa’s 1604 forced relocation into the account, and compare state patronage with the Ottoman case.
Open the lacquer case and its additional views. Its date falls after Karim Khan’s death. A practical object and an idealized courtly image do not establish the same facts.

conclusion: Courts could commission beautiful work while makers also worked for markets and urban institutions. Silk connected farming, skilled production and commerce with coercion and unequal power. A literary painting, official emblem and practical case reveal different things; none can stand alone for everyone’s experience.

evidence.prompt: Which account best respects both the silk evidence and the history of New Julfa?

options.text: Luxury production involved several forms of work, and New Julfa’s later commercial importance does not make the 1604 deportation voluntary.
options.feedback: The workshop account identifies multiple producers and skills. Ghougassian separately documents forced relocation, later settlement and unequal privileges.

options.text: A beautiful carpet proves everyone involved was prosperous and free to move.
options.feedback: An object’s quality does not establish its makers’ freedom or the conditions of every worker. The documented deportation directly challenges that inference.

options.text: The name Polonaise proves the carpet was woven in Poland.
options.feedback: The catalogue explains the older misattribution and identifies Iranian production centers, while leaving this individual carpet’s precise workshop unresolved.
